Bodzanow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Bodzanów, Poland

Demolished. Bodzanów, granted town rights in 1351 under Chełmno law, saw larger-scale Jewish settlement develop in the 18th century, initially burying their dead in nearby Wyszogród before establishing an independent kehilla in 1830; population reached about 38% by the 19th century. A 1922 fire in the town led to Jews being wrongly blamed. By 1939, about 1,300 Jews lived there; a March 1941 deportation sent residents through Działdowo to the Szydłów and Częstochowa ghettos, with others reaching Nowy Dwór and the Ciechanów district before most died at Treblinka and Auschwitz. This cemetery, most likely established at the end of the 18th century, was probably closed in 1938 when the community established a new cemetery in nearby Chodków. Germans completely destroyed the site during WWII, repurposing tombstones for street paving; Poland formally closed the cemetery for burials in 1964. A 2004 monument, designed by Jolanta Leszczyńska and initiated by the local Social Committee for the Construction of the Obelisk with the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage, now stands alongside two recovered tombstones (dated 1923 and 1937).
